claims.text: High-entropy alloys containing a sufficient amount of Al, Ti, or Cr develop a continuous and adherent oxide layer at high temperature.
The protective oxide may be a spinel phase.
Al, Ti, or Cr preferentially oxidize relative to the other alloy constituents.
The oxide layer acts as a self-healing barrier that significantly reduces further oxidation.
The proposed initial HEA has a multiphase microstructure.
The proposed HEA can be synthesized through a powder-based route.
The elemental or powder precursors are uniformly mixed.
Exposure for several hours at 800–900 °C in air permits formation and stabilization of the protective oxide.
A continuous, adherent oxide film forms preferentially along reactive-element-enriched regions.
The oxide film retards diffusion of oxygen into the bulk alloy.
Retarded oxygen diffusion lowers the oxidation rate relative to alloys lacking sufficient reactive-element content.
Increasing reactive-element content produces a more uniform, dense, and adherent oxide layer.
Increasing reactive-element content reduces oxidation weight gain or the parabolic oxidation-rate constant.
Increasing reactive-element content reduces oxide spallation and improves surface integrity.
A baseline alloy with minimal reactive-element content forms a discontinuous or non-protective oxide and oxidizes faster.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to oxidation at approximately 800–900 °C over exposures lasting several hours.
The mechanism may fail at lower temperatures or at extremely high temperatures where spallation or other degradation modes dominate.
Prior analogous systems support a qualitative role for reactive-element content in promoting adherent oxide formation.
